title: A Safehouse for the Cover
premise: Wren Nakamura's security firm is hired to protect a whistleblower who was supposedly aboard a flight that officially never existed — a plane carrying evidence that a coalition of three governments laundered arms through a humanitarian corridor. As the flight's records are erased mid-air and its surviving passenger becomes a target, Wren discovers his own firm helped build the cover-up, and the 'incident' that broke his sleep was its first test run. Guided by a ragged team of exiled analysts, a disgraced air traffic controller, and the assassin who defects rather than kill the last witness, Wren smuggles the truth to an international tribunal in Lagos. The book ends with the evidence landing publicly, Wren's firm dismantled from within, and Wren finally sleeping through the night — not because justice was served, but because he stopped needing permission to believe it could be.
about_author: V. M. Oyelaran is a former logistics consultant who spent a decade moving people and secrets across West African borders before turning to fiction. They write from Lagos and Lisbon, and claim their best plot ideas come from airport departure boards.

chapters.title: The Client Nobody Names
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A private security contractor running on four hours of sleep a night takes a lucrative, vague job protecting a nervous woman named Ilse who claims to have been on a flight that doesn't exist. The beat: professional detachment masking dread, as Wren recognizes the shape of a job he's done before — the ones that end badly.

chapters.title: Flight 409, Deleted
chapters.summary: Alternating Wren and Ilse POV. Mid-consultation, every trace of Ilse's flight vanishes from databases worldwide while it is still listed as airborne. Wren's own firm's systems scrub themselves. The beat: vertigo — the ground truth of reality shifting under both characters at once.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He moves Ilse to a company safehouse and discovers the security contract's fine print gives his employer unilateral termination rights — over the client, and possibly over Wren. The beat: paranoia hardening into resolve as he starts keeping a private, paper-only record.

chapters.title: The Man with the Luggage Tag
chapters.summary: Assassin Corvus's POV, unnamed until the end. A meticulous killer is assigned the witness and studies Wren's routines, noting with unexpected respect the contractor's sleepless discipline. The beat: cold professionalism laced with a hairline crack of doubt about who issues his orders.

chapters.title: Paper Doesn't Sync
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. In the safehouse she reveals what she carried: flight manifests proving arms moved through a protected aid corridor, signed by officials in three governments. Wren realizes his firm built the logistics that made the cover-up possible. The beat: betrayal, and the first flicker of found-family warmth between the two.

chapters.title: The Incident, Replayed
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, flashback-heavy. The job two years ago that broke his sleep — a protection detail that ended with a client's death he was ordered to write off as accidental — is revealed as the cover-up's dress rehearsal. The beat: guilt reframed as complicity; Wren stops being a bystander in his own story.

chapters.title: Three Flags, One Shadow
chapters.summary: Corvus's POV. His handlers, representing three governments, begin contradicting each other, each assuming the other ordered the witness's death. Corvus realizes he is the loose end. The beat: the assassin discovers he is also being hunted.

chapters.title: The Controller Who Watched It Land
chapters.summary: New POV: Amara, a suspended air traffic controller who tracked Flight 409 to an unlisted airstrip and was fired for it. Wren finds her through an exile network of analysts and fixers. The beat: cautious alliance; the team that will carry the book begins to assemble.

chapters.title: Safehouse Protocol
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A routine check reveals the firm knows where Ilse is; Wren burns the safehouse and moves her through Lagos's underbelly using skills from his old logistics life. The beat: competence under fire, and the first time Wren chooses the client over the contract.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Corvus's POV. Cornered by his own employers, Corvus makes contact with Wren — not to trade, but to offer the one thing he owns: the kill order itself, signed and dated. The beat: uneasy truce; two professionals negotiating trust in a language of leverage.

chapters.title: What the Manifests Weigh
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. The team authenticates the documents and maps a route to the international tribunal sitting in Lagos — but learns the tribunal's lead prosecutor is on the cover-up's payroll. The beat: hope undercut; the law itself is compromised, forcing the question of justice outside the law.

chapters.title: The Firm Calls Home
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. His mentor and firm founder, Okafor, offers Wren a clean exit: walk away, keep his license, forget Ilse. Wren hears in the offer the same voice that ordered the cover-up of the incident. The beat: grief for the father-figure, and refusal — the moral pivot of the book.

chapters.title: Night Market
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. A document handoff in a crowded market goes wrong; Amara is wounded, and Ilse freezes, revealing her survivor's guilt over colleagues who died aboard 409. The beat: found family tested by failure; Wren carries Amara out while Ilse finally fights instead of hiding.

chapters.title: Corvus, Unemployed
chapters.summary: Corvus's POV. Officially disavowed, he survives an ambush meant to erase him and delivers the signed kill order to Wren — the first hard evidence naming names. The beat: the assassin's cold architecture cracking into something like purpose.

chapters.title: The Long Layover
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hiding in an airport hotel, the team plans the tribunal gambit while governments close in; Wren and Corvus trade watch shifts, two insomniacs guarding the only sleeping witness. The beat: quiet before the storm; tenderness in the margins.

chapters.title: Okafor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. The team cracks the firm's financials and finds the incident — Wren's old failure — was a deliberate sacrifice play, with Okafor's signature. Wren reads it in silence. The beat: rage transmuted into clarity; the enemy is no longer a system but a man Wren loved.

chapters.title: Doors That Lock from Outside
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse is taken in a coordinated raid by agents of all three governments, each believing the others ordered it. Wren realizes the abduction was the plan: kill her in custody and blame a rival state. The beat: desperation; the clock becomes audible.

chapters.title: The Exchange at the Airstrip
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, climax begins. Wren and Corvus infiltrate the unlisted airstrip where Flight 409 landed, using Corvus's old credentials and Amara's knowledge of the tower. The beat: controlled chaos; every skill the team built pays off in a single night.

chapters.title: Terminal Velocity
chapters.summary: Alternating Wren and Corvus POV, climax. Ilse is recovered, Okafor confronts Wren on the tarmac and dies — by his own hand or a handler's bullet, never fully resolved — as the team fights to get Ilse and the manifests to the tribunal before dawn. The beat: sacrifice, fury, and Wren choosing the witness over revenge.

chapters.title: Exhibit A
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. In the tribunal chamber, the manifests, the kill order, and Ilse's testimony land in open session, broadcast past the reach of three governments. The beat: catharsis — justice arriving not through power but through stubbornness and found family.

chapters.title: Aftermaths and Alibis
chapters.summary: Corvus's POV. The firm dissolves, governments shuffle blame, and Corvus walks out of a hearing a free man with no name worth arresting. He leaves Wren a paper luggage tag — the only receipt for what they survived. The beat: bittersweet release; the assassin learning to exist without orders.

chapters.title: A Safehouse for the Cover
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. Months later, Wren runs a tiny, honest security practice with Amara and Ilse; the safehouse is now a home. On a quiet night he locks the door, lies down, and sleeps until morning. The beat: peace earned, not granted — the final answer to the incident.
